newsitem.title: GERMANY: Villeroy expects to swing to profit in 97.
newsitem.headline: Villeroy expects to swing to profit in 97.

text.p: German tableware and bathroom fittings group Villeroy & Boch on Monday forecast it would swing to profit in 1997 after orders and sales picked up in the first four months despite ongoing sluggish industry conditions.

"For the year 1997 we are optimistic that we can again present positive results," Villeroy management board chairman Joerg Grueneisen told a news conference, adding however that sales were expected to remain largely steady at 1996 levels.
The group's shares benefited from the upbeat outlook, climbing nearly two percent in bourse trade to 260 marks ($154), outpacing the broader market's 1.5 percent rise.

After the Villeroy group last year reported a net loss of 103 million marks after 1995's 34.1 million mark profit, largely due to a one-time restructuring charge, Grueneisen said the 250-year old group had readied itself for the future.

By taking a 114.1 million mark charge to overhaul all of its three main business areas, tiles, sanitary products and tableware, Grueneisen said "we are creating a platform for continuous growth of our profitability with this strategy."

Besides digesting the restructuring charge, Villeroy last year also faced ongoing sluggish consumer demand and a shift to lower priced goods which helped dent turnover by two percent to 1.453 billion marks, Grueneisen said.
Sales of tiles climbed nearly three percent to 517.4 million marks trailed by a 2.4 percent rise in tableware product sales to 490.8 million marks.

Tableware sales received an extra boost from improved exchange rates as the mark's depreciation against international currencies, particularly the dollar, made German exports cheaper abroad, Grueneisen said.
But sales in sanitary fittings slipped over 11 percent to 444.9 million marks, hit hard by a drop in the construction and renovation industries, Grueneisen added.

Group income from ordinary activities dropped over 60 percent to 33 million marks, Villeroy said. The group's net cash flow stood at 92.7 million marks in 1996 compared with 155.1 million marks a year earlier.
Unsatisfactory 1996 results forced Villeroy to omit its dividend for 1996 after paying out 6.50 marks for common shares and 7.50 marks per preference share the year before.
Villeroy had already cut its 1995 dividend payment as it was hurt by higher production costs in the domestic market and the economic recession which hit in the early 1990s.
Looking ahead Grueneisen said, "we expect to see noticeable effects from the initiated promgrammes this year."

As part of the overhaul, Villeroy said it would continue to cut costs by transferring production to cheaper sites like its plants in Hungary and Romania as well as adjusting its portfolio to market demands.
Similarly the group plans to expand in eastern Europe, Asia and the North America, targeting these markets as areas where higher sales could be achieved.
Although there are no signs of a marked recovery in the construction industry, Villeroy said that results in the first four months of this year already showed an improvement.

"In total sales in the three business areas are were slightly above year ago levels in the first four months of 1997 while orders clearly outpaced year-ago levels," Grueneisen said. Similarly "income from ordinary activities was clearly above year-ago levels," Grueneisen added.
